lesson.title: No Function Can Skip a Value: The Intermediate Value Theorem
lesson.summary: If a function is continuous on a closed interval, it must take on every value between its endpoint values at least once, a fact that guarantees roots exist even when you cannot solve for them exactly.
lesson.body:
Continuity on an entire interval means the graph over that interval is one connected, unbroken curve, with no gaps to jump across. The Intermediate Value Theorem, often abbreviated IVT, turns that intuitive picture into a precise and powerful guarantee: a continuous curve cannot skip over a value without actually passing through it somewhere along the way.

Formally, the theorem states that if f is continuous on the closed interval [a, b], and N is any number between f(a) and f(b), then there exists at least one number c in the open interval (a, b) such that f(c) = N. Both hypotheses matter. Continuity must hold on the entire closed interval, not just at the endpoints, and if f had even a single jump discontinuity somewhere in between, the graph really could leap over the value N without ever equaling it.

The most common use of the theorem is a special case with N = 0, sometimes called the sign-change corollary: if f is continuous on [a, b] and f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, then f must have at least one root, a value c in (a, b) with f(c) = 0. This gives a way to guarantee a solution exists even when there is no algebraic method to solve for it exactly.

For a worked example, consider f(x) = x^3 - x - 1 and the question of whether it has a root between x = 1 and x = 2. Since f is a polynomial, it is continuous on the entire real line, including the closed interval [1, 2]. Evaluating the endpoints gives f(1) = 1 - 1 - 1 = -1 and f(2) = 8 - 2 - 1 = 5. Because f(1) = -1 is negative and f(2) = 5 is positive, and 0 lies between -1 and 5, the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees some c in (1, 2) with f(c) = 0. As a numerical check, this cubic does have a real root near 1.3247, a value known as the plastic number, satisfying the equation exactly, but the theorem lets you conclude a root exists in that interval without ever needing to find its precise value.

It is worth emphasizing what the theorem does and does not provide. It is a pure existence statement: it guarantees a value c exists, but it gives no formula for finding c. In practice, this existence guarantee is combined with a numerical technique called the bisection method, which repeatedly halves the interval, checking the sign of f at the midpoint and applying the IVT again on whichever half still brackets a sign change, closing in on the root to any desired precision.

The idea shows up outside of pure algebra as well. If the outdoor temperature was 65 degrees at 9am and 78 degrees at noon, and temperature varies continuously over time, then the IVT guarantees the temperature was exactly 70 degrees at some moment in between, even though nobody was watching the thermometer at that instant. This is the same reasoning, applied to a physical rather than algebraic function, that makes continuity such a useful working assumption in modeling real processes.
